newsitem.title: UK: Labour promises new Britain for new century.
newsitem.headline: Labour promises new Britain for new century.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government on Sunday pledged a radical programme of change for the millennium while the defeated Conservatives took up positions for the battle to lead their shattered party.
Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott, still savouring the novelty of office after 18 years in opposition, said Britain faced a "bumpy ride" ahead.
Newly elected Prime Minister Tony Blair planned to shake up the nation in the same way he overhauled the Labour Party, Prescott said.

Blair now has a stunning 179-seat majority, justifying his crusade to modernise the Labour party by junking old socialist dogma and silencing critics on the left. With such strong backing in parliament, he is free to enact controversial legislation and fulfil his pledge of "radical centrist" rule.

"He wants to see a new kind of Britain going into a new millennium and he'll have as much effect on British political life as he's had on the Labour Party in the last two or three years," Prescott said on BBC television. "Quite frankly, it may well be a bumpy ride but I'm looking forward to it."

Blair was on Sunday putting the finishing touches to his ministerial team after Saturday's announcement of a radical cabinet containing five women, one avowedly homosexual minister, National Heritage Secretary Chris Smith, and one blind minister, Education Secretary David Blunkett.

Labour's defeated Conservative rivals meanwhile jostled for position in a leadership race expected early this summer following John Major's announcement he was stepping down after his party's worst electoral defeat since 1832.

The race was thrown wide open at the weekend when Michael Heseltine, one of the party's few remaining big guns after the election debacle, announced he would not be standing. He had been admitted to hospital suffering from chest pains.
Former social security secretary Peter Lilley, a rightwing anti-European, put himself forward as the best man to reunite the party and said he had received an avalanche of support.

"I am the best-placed to reunite, rebuild and renew the party," he told the Mail on Sunday newspaper. "We must restore our rapport with the country and end the caricature of the Tories (Conservatives) as hard-faced men without a social conscience."
Former Welsh Secretary John Redwood, another fierce opponent of further integration with Europe, was on the verge of announcing he would stand.
"It is very likely I will run," he told Independent Television. "The main task is to win back the trust of the British people through local government and show we are a party worth joining again."

Former finance minister Kenneth Clarke has already declared that he will stand. Other possible candidates are former Welsh Secretary William Hague, aged just 36, and former health secretary Stephen Dorrell.

Europe was the issue that tore the Conservative Party apart and with more than half of the remaining 165 Conservative members of parliament still displaying anti-European tendencies, the issue is unlikely to go away.'

"The troubles of the last two or three years have entirely been caused by Europe. It is a kind of cancer at the heart of the party. Some people are quite obsessed by it, they are quite incapable of agreeing upon it," Clarke said.
Clarke sought to boost his credentials with the irascible right by offering members a free vote on joining a single European currency and other big European issues.
But Lilley said this was not realistic as the opposition had to offer a coherent view on such important matters.
